title: Jumps, landings and power
summary: Why jumping starts with landing, how jumps are counted, and the rules for pogos, back-to-back jumps, landing drills, the Trap Bar Jump and med ball throws.

p: Every jump ends with a landing, and every brake on court looks a lot like a landing too. So your programme builds soft, solid landings first, then makes the jumps higher and faster. The research behind this lesson is on tennis players, and we found no padel trial, so we use the same movement logic.
The path goes like this: landings, pogos and short hops over a line, jumps where you land and hold, and last, short runs of back-to-back jumps. A good landing looks like this:
list: On a two-foot landing, both feet hit the ground together. On a one-foot landing, the other foot doesn't touch down.
Soft and quiet: hips go back and your knees and ankles bend. No stiff, straight-legged landing.
Your knee stays over your toes, not caving in.
You're still within 1 second and you hold it for as long as your session says.
No extra step or hop and no grabbing anything. Shoulders stay over your hips.
sections.callout: On jumps where your session says to hold the landing, only jump as far as you can land cleanly. These landing cues are standard coaching practice, not the result of a separate study.

p: Your programme counts jumps in ground contacts. Each time you land after leaving the ground is one contact. In your sessions each contact is called a “jump”, so 20 warm-up pogos are “20 jumps”.

Why count them? Jumps need to build up slowly, just like weights. A review of seven low-quality studies in children before puberty (aged 5 to 14) found that two sessions a week, starting from about 50 to 60 jumps a session, worked well, and that's why your jumps usually sit in your gym sessions.
list: Landing on two feet together: 1 contact. Landing on one foot: 1 contact for that leg.
In a back-to-back run, every touch counts. 10 pogos means 10 contacts.
A jump that ends with a land and hold is 1 contact too.
Landing without a jump, like a Snap Down, Box Drop or Step-Off Landing, is landing practice and doesn't count as a jump.
Warm-up pogos count. Running, skips and ladder steps don't.
sections.callout: Under 16: 60 jumps a session at most. This is the course's own rule, not a study result. If you're under 16, your programme already sticks to it.

sections.h: Pogos and short hops: for every age
p: Pogo Jumps and Lateral Line Hops are short, fast jumps. Your ankle works like a spring and your knee only bends a little. They're the base for your split step and quick feet.
Everyone does these as written, under-16s too. The warm-up pogos in your gym sessions are the same kind, and they're normal practice, not a trick a study has proved.
list: Land on the balls of your feet, not your heels.
Short and low. The goal is to get off the ground fast, not to go high.
Light, quiet feet.
Don't bend your knees a lot to jump higher.

sections.h: Back-to-back jumps: later in your programme
p: Later on, some jumps come back to back with short ground contacts, like Hurdle Hops, Continuous Broad Jumps and back-to-back Lateral Bounds. Hold the last landing of each run.
This is the last step on the jump path, so it only comes once you've built up landings and jumps with a hold.
list: Each set is one run: jumps with no pause between them.
Short contact. As soon as your feet touch, get off the ground again.
Heels slamming down, or a long pause in the middle? End the run there.
Don't set the hurdle higher than your session says.
sections.warn: Under 16: 4 jumps in a row at most, and 3 at most for single-leg jumps and Lateral Bounds. Hurdles 15 cm at most. If you're under 16, your programme already uses these numbers. Pogos and short line hops don't fall under this limit. These numbers are the course's own rules, not study results.

p: Some sessions have a landing drill in the jump section. 16 and over: a Box Drop from a 30 cm box. Under 16: a Step-Off Landing from a 20 cm step.

In both, you step off (don't jump off), land on two feet and hold still for 2 seconds. There's no jump after the landing, and it doesn't count as a jump. The heights and the age split at 16 are the course's own rules, not study results.

Depth jumps and drop jumps, where you step off a box and jump straight away, are advanced. Nobody under 16 does them, and you should never add them yourself. They only go in your programme if Amir puts them there.
sections.warn: Box Jump: always step down from the box, never jump down. Under 16, the box is 30 cm at most.
sections.callout: A Box Drop is landing practice. Step off, land quietly and hold still.

p: Players 16 and over may do Trap Bar Jumps before the main lift. You jump holding a light trap bar. The goal is speed, not weight.
The weight is light and your session tells you how much. Jump as high as you can and land softly in the same foot position. If your jump height drops, end the set.
Under-16s don't do weighted jumps. That's the course's own rule, not a study result.
sections.callout: If the weight slows your jump down, it's too heavy for this drill.

sections.h: Med ball throws and your serve
p: Med ball throws train fast rotation in the same order as a shot: legs, hips, trunk and then arm. They're part of your gym sessions, and later on overhead throws that look like a serve come in too.

To be honest, in one review of studies, throws on their own often didn't change serve or shot speed, and that review was on players after puberty and adults, not juniors. Programmes that mixed leg jumps with upper-body jump or throwing work did make young players' serves faster, so see throws as one part of the whole programme, not a fix for your serve.
list: Throw hard and fast. The throw is for speed.
Start the movement from your legs and hips, not just your arm.
16 and over: a 2 to 3 kg ball. Under 16: 1 to 2 kg. A lighter ball moves faster.
These weights are practice, not trial results.

p: Jumps and throws don't have an RPE. The goal is your best quality, so every rep is flat out and clean.
list: Take the full rest in your session so the next rep is just as fast and high.
Quality dropped, like a loud landing, your knee caving in or a shorter jump? End that set and don't make up the reps.
Don't add anything to your session. No extra jumps, and no higher box or hurdle.
In lighter weeks there are fewer jumps, but they're still flat out.
sections.callout: During a growth spurt, we cut jumps back as a precaution. It isn't a proven effect. In one review, boys aged about 13 to 16 gained less jump height. The lesson “Growth spurts: a guide for players and parents” shows you how.
